Priority improvements, ordered by impact:

1. Put the validation evidence at the center. The plan itself admits the biggest weakness is that scores are unvalidated against clinical scales (MDS-UPDRS tremor items). Do not bury this. Present a concrete validation plan: sample size, comparator (UPDRS ratings by blinded clinicians, possibly wearable ground truth), accuracy targets, timeline, and cost. Even a small preliminary dataset from the existing pilot (e.g., correlation between app scores and the clinic's own ratings) would convert a stated weakness into early evidence.

2. Replace vague claims with quantified, sourced data. 'Close to one million,' 'several thousand neurologists,' and 'grows quickly' need citations and numbers. Build a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM: number of target clinics x patients per clinic x realistic enrollment rate x price. Show how 200 patients across 10 clinics yields about $50K ARR (200 x $20 x 12 = $48K) and what the path beyond that looks like. The current projection is a single data point, not a model.

3. Resolve the reimbursement and regulatory questions or show a credible plan. Identify the applicable CPT codes for remote physiologic monitoring (e.g., 99453/99454/99457/99458) and whether video-derived data qualifies, since the whole clinic-pays model leans on this. State whether the product is likely to be a medical device under FDA rules (software as a medical device, De Novo/510(k) vs. wellness positioning), and how the claims you make ('flags significant changes,' supports treatment decisions) affect that. Clarify the HIPAA position: BAAs, encryption, retention of patient video, consent, and cloud vendor compliance. 'We need to research this' is acceptable only if paired with a dated plan and owner.

4. Strengthen the pilot story. The paid pilot is your best asset but is described in two sentences. Add: number of patients, duration, adherence rate (how many patients actually record daily), clinician usage of the dashboard, any change in clinical decisions, and direct quotes or a letter of support. Adherence and clinician workflow fit are the true adoption risks; show data on them.

5. Sharpen competitive positioning with specifics. Name competitors (e.g., wrist-worn FDA-cleared devices, existing PD digital biomarker platforms, smartphone-based assessment apps) and compare on validation status, cost, hardware, and reimbursement. Be honest that 'no hardware' is an advantage in cost but a risk in accuracy, and explain how you will defend against better-funded entrants adding a camera-based mode. Articulate a moat: proprietary labeled dataset, clinic integrations, longitudinal data.

6. Address technical and usability risks. Video-based tremor estimation depends on lighting, camera angle, framerate, and hand occlusion. Describe how the pipeline handles variability, quality checks, and failure modes. Also address video storage cost and privacy: could you process on-device or store only extracted features plus short clips to cut cost and risk? Provide unit economics (cost per patient per month for hosting vs. $15-25 price) and gross margin.

7. Fix the team and structure gaps with a plan, not an acknowledgment. The lack of a physician and regulatory expertise is correctly flagged; go further by naming the advisor (with permission), defining their role, and listing the specific advisors you will recruit and by when. Settle the founder equity split and legal entity before or alongside submission, since unresolved ownership is a red flag to funders. State commitment level (full-time after graduation) and any vesting.

8. Make the ask concrete. Give a use-of-funds table with amounts and timeline: validation study cost, legal/compliance, website, pilot expansion, and what milestone each unlocks (e.g., publishable validation result, 5 paying clinics, X patients). Define success metrics for the next 6-12 months. Funders respond to a clear 'this money buys this proof point' narrative.

9. Clean up presentation. The plan reads as candid but informal in places ('alot,' 'effects' vs. 'affects,' 'it is partly justified'). Proofread, tighten the executive summary into a crisp problem-solution-traction-ask opening, and add a few visuals (dashboard screenshot, trend chart, workflow diagram, financial table). Add a basic web presence, since not having a website undermines credibility with clinics and reviewers.

10. Reframe the data-partnership idea. Pharma data licensing is a speculative upside that raises consent and privacy concerns; either develop it with a clear consent model and evidence of demand, or move it to a brief future-opportunity note so it does not dilute the core clinic-subscription story.

Net: the idea and founder-problem fit are strong and the paid pilot is real traction. The submission would improve most by converting stated unknowns (validation, reimbursement, regulation, market size) into specific, dated plans with early evidence, and by quantifying pilot results and unit economics.

Business plan text:

Tremorlog
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Tremorlog, a student startup from our university
The Problem
Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder which effects close to one million
people in the United States, and tremor is one of the most visible and disruptive symptoms. The
problem is that the way doctors currently track it is very outdated. A patient with Parkinson's
typically sees their neurologist every three to six months, and the appointment is short.
During that time the doctor observes the patient, asks questions, and makes a judgement about
how medication is working. But Parkinson's symptoms fluctuate alot during the day and from week
to week, depending on medication timing, sleep, stress and many other factors. So what the
neurologist sees in the room is only a snapshot, and often not a representative one. Patients
are asked to remember how they did over the past months, and memory is unreliable especially
when the disease can also effect cognition. Some patients keep paper diaries but these are
inconsistent and subjective. As a result medication decisions are sometimes made with
incomplete information, and worsening symptoms may go unnoticed for months. There is a real gap
in remote monitoring of movement disorders, unlike conditions such as diabetes where home
devices provide continuous data.
Our Solution
Tremorlog is a web application that fills this gap in a simple way. The patient, or a
caregiver, opens the app on a phone, tablet or laptop and records a short video, around thirty
seconds, of their hands at rest and holding a posture, following simple on screen prompts. This
takes about two minutes and is meant to be done once a day at a consistent time. Our software
then processes the video using computer vision to estimate tremor amplitude and frequency and
generates a daily score. Over time the app builds a trend line which the patient can see too.
On the other side, the neurologist has a clinician dashboard that shows each patient's trend,
flags significant changes, and lets them review the actual video clips if they want to. Before
an appointment the doctor can see weeks of data rather than relying on a single observation. We
think this makes visits more productive and could allow earlier adjustments to treatment. We
chose a web app rather than a native mobile app so that there is nothing to download, which
matters because many Parkinson's patients are older and not always comfortable with technology.
Market
There are approximately one million people living with Parkinson's in the US and about sixty
thousand new diagnoses each year. Beyond Parkinson's the same approach could extend to
essential tremor and other movement disorders which would make the market several times bigger.
There are also roughly several thousand practicing neurologists and movement disorder
specialists. The remote patient monitoring market is growing quickly, driven by changes in how
telehealth is reimbursed and by greater acceptance from both patients and clinicians after the
pandemic. We have not yet done a full bottom up market sizing but if even a small percentage of
Parkinson's patients were paying a monthly fee through their clinic this would be a meaningful
business. Our initial target is small and mid sized neurology practices and movement disorder
clinics because they can make purchasing decisions faster than large hospital systems.
Business Model
Our plan is to sell subscriptions to clinics, not to individual patients. The clinic pays a
monthly fee per active patient enrolled, which we are currently testing at a price in the range
of fifteen to twenty five dollars per patient per month. This is partly justified because
remote monitoring services may be billable by clinics under existing reimbursement codes,
although we have not yet confirmed exactly which codes apply to our product and this is
something we need to research with a healthcare reimbursement expert. Secondary revenue could
come later from anonymized data partnerships with pharmaceutical companies running clinical

trials who need objective symptom measures, but this raises privacy questions which we will
address carefully and only with patient consent. Our costs are mainly cloud hosting and video
storage, which are significant because video files are large, plus development time.
Competition
There are other players in this space. Some companies have wearable sensors that measure
tremor, and one or two larger companies have FDA cleared devices worn on the wrist. These are
more clinically validated than we are, but they require buying and shipping hardware, are
expensive and patients must wear them. There are also general telehealth platforms which allow
video visits but do not give continuous or quantitative data. Finally there are symptom diary
apps which are cheap but rely on self reporting. Our advantage is that we need no special
hardware, only a camera that the patient already owns, and so our cost to deploy is very low.
Our weakness is that video based measurement is probably less accurate than a dedicated sensor,
and we have not yet formally validated our scores against clinical rating scales. We know this
is the biggest question mark about our product.
Team
Priyanka Venkataraman leads product and clinical relationships. She is a senior studying
neuroscience and has volunteered at a movement disorders clinic, where the idea started after
she saw how little information doctors had between visits. Desmond Okafor-Reyes is our lead
engineer, studying computer science, and he built the prototype including the video analysis
pipeline. Callum Tishkoff handles business operations, finance and the company registration,
and is studying business administration. We do not currently have a physician on the team, but
we have been in conversation with a neurologist who has agreed to informally advise us. We
recognize that a clinical advisor and someone with regulatory experience are needed.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype that handles video capture,
scoring and the clinician dashboard, and registered the company. Our first client, a small
neurology practice, has paid for a pilot covering a limited number of patients, which gave us
our first revenue and a lot of useful feedback. The legal entity itself is still not fully
formed, and we need to sort out the formal structure and ownership split between founders.
Revenue to date is very small, only the pilot fee, and costs have been mostly covered by the
founders personally plus small savings. We project that with ten clinics and around two hundred
patients we could reach approximately fifty thousand dollars in annual recurring revenue,
though this depends on assumptions about pricing and adoption that we have not tested widely.
We also do not yet have a website.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding to support three things. First, to run a validation study
comparing our tremor scores with standard clinical ratings, ideally with the help of a
university medical partner. Second, to get legal advice on forming the company properly and on
privacy and health data rules including what compliance is needed for handling patient video.
Third, to build a basic website and expand the pilot to several more clinics. Beyond money we
would value mentorship from people with healthcare startup experience, introductions to
neurologists, and guidance on the regulatory pathway. We believe Tremorlog addresses a real and
underserved need and we are committed to working on it after graduation.
Question: What can the team do to improve their written submission?
